questions.question: Which assessment best detects an early pressure-related change in deeply pigmented skin?
choices: Look only for bright redness
Compare with nearby tissue and assess persistent color change, temperature, firmness, edema, and pain
Rely only on the pressure-risk score
Wait until the skin opens
questions.explanation: Early pressure damage may not appear bright red or show visible blanching in deeply pigmented skin. Local temperature, firmness, pain, edema, and persistent discoloration are important comparative cues.

questions.question: The RN finds an intact, tender, nonblanching area over the heel. What is the priority action?
choices: Massage the area vigorously
Relieve pressure, offload the heel, complete and document the assessment, and implement the prevention pathway
Place the heel directly on a heating pad
Wait for blistering before intervening
questions.explanation: Persistent nonblanching change over a bony prominence indicates tissue injury risk. Immediate pressure relief and an individualized prevention and follow-up plan can limit further damage; massage may worsen injury.

questions.question: A wound bed is fully covered by slough and eschar, so the depth cannot be seen. How should the RN classify the finding under the pressure-injury staging system?
choices: Stage 1
Stage 2
Automatically Stage 4
Unstageable until enough obscuring tissue is removed or otherwise evaluated according to policy
questions.explanation: When slough or eschar obscures the full extent of tissue loss, the depth cannot be confirmed. It is documented as unstageable rather than guessed as Stage 3 or 4.

questions.question: Which skin finding requires the most immediate action?
choices: A stable freckle present for years
Dry skin on both lower legs
A rapidly spreading rash with lip swelling, wheezing, and hypotension
A small bruise after a blood draw
questions.explanation: Widespread rash with angioedema, respiratory symptoms, and hypotension is an airway and circulation emergency. The RN initiates immediate emergency assessment and response.

questions.question: Why is skin turgor alone a poor way to assess dehydration in an older adult?
choices: Older adults cannot become dehydrated
Age-related loss of elasticity can alter turgor, so it must be combined with mucosa, intake and output, weight, vital signs, perfusion, and other findings
Turgor measures oxygen saturation
Turgor is valid only on the heel
questions.explanation: Reduced skin elasticity can make turgor misleading in older adults. Hydration assessment requires a cluster of subjective, examination, trend, and laboratory findings when available.

questions.question: What is the best way to assess skin beneath a removable medical device?
choices: Leave the device untouched for the entire hospitalization
When clinically safe, remove or reposition it according to policy, inspect and palpate contact areas, then restore prescribed therapy correctly
Inspect only after the client reports severe pain
Place extra layers under every device without checking fit
questions.explanation: Medical devices can conceal pressure, moisture, and friction injury. The RN protects the therapy while directly assessing contact areas at the required frequency and correcting risk according to policy.

questions.question: Which description of a skin lesion is most objective?
choices: Suspicious rash
Bad-looking mole
Single 0.8-cm asymmetric dark-brown macule on left upper back with irregular border and two color tones; client reports recent enlargement
Skin cancer present
questions.explanation: Objective description records number, size, morphology, location, symmetry, border, color, and evolution. It supports evaluation without substituting an unconfirmed diagnosis.

questions.question: A client has new widespread petechiae, fever, hypotension, and confusion. How should the RN respond?
choices: Apply moisturizer and reassess next week
Treat the systemic cluster as urgent, assess ABCs and perfusion, and activate the appropriate response
Massage the petechiae to test blanching
Assume the spots are normal bruises
questions.explanation: Petechiae accompanied by fever, hypotension, and altered mental status may signal a serious systemic process. The RN prioritizes stabilization and urgent evaluation rather than isolated skin care.

questions.question: Assistive personnel report a new dark, tender area on the sacrum during hygiene. What should the RN do?
choices: Ask the assistant to stage it
Personally assess color, temperature, firmness, blanching when appropriate, integrity, size, pain and pressure risk, then initiate and evaluate the plan
Document normal skin because it is not bright red
Wait until the next scheduled weekly assessment
questions.explanation: The RN validates new skin findings, determines the clinical meaning and urgency, implements pressure relief and other indicated measures, and communicates or consults according to policy.

questions.question: Which skin documentation is most useful for comparison?
choices: Heel looks bad
Pressure sore noted
Right heel intact with 2.0 × 1.5 cm persistent violaceous area, warmer and firmer than adjacent tissue, tender 4/10; heel offloaded and wound-resource RN notified
Skin checked
questions.explanation: Specific documentation identifies location, measurements, color, integrity, comparative temperature and firmness, pain, intervention, and communication. It avoids vague wording and unsupported staging.
